title: Failure of strong quadratic growth in unregularized sparse control of a critical wave equation
description: A critical-wave sparse-control example has a unique optimizer but no strong L² quadratic growth after removal of the quadratic control penalty.
abstract: We give an explicit counterexample to retaining ordinary critical-cone strict positivity and strong control-L² quadratic growth after removing quadratic control regularization from the energy-critical quintic-wave problem of Kunisch and Meinlschmidt. On the three-dimensional unit ball, zero is the unique global optimizer for a sufficiently small positive pointwise control cap. Its ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict condition is vacuous, but feasible controls converging in L∞ have objective gap o(‖u‖²L²). Nearby radial terminal targets admit global optimizers, and every such optimizer has L² displacement divided by target displacement tending to infinity. Local L¹ quadratic growth survives. The construction realizes the established concentration and noncoercivity mechanism in the actual nonlinear source model, using classical wave estimates.
plain_language: In optimal control, a control is an input chosen to make a system behave as desired. This paper studies a nonlinear wave equation, where the objective balances a desired final wave profile against penalties on the state and on the amount of control used.

A useful stability property says that moving away from the best control raises the objective by at least a fixed multiple of the squared distance. In this example, doing nothing is the unique global optimum, but increasingly short, small pulses have an objective penalty much smaller than their squared L² size. Uniqueness therefore does not supply that stronger growth property.

The striking feature is that the ordinary critical-cone test still holds: its cone contains only zero, so there are no nonzero directions on which the strict test can fail. The concentrating pulses reveal what this test misses. A weaker L¹ quadratic-growth estimate survives, and the paper also bounds how optimizers respond to nearby terminal targets.
result: The model is the real defocusing quintic wave equation yₜₜ − Δy + y⁵ = u on the unit ball B in ℝ³, with zero initial data, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and final time 1. Controls lie in L²(0,1;L²(B)) and obey ‖u(t)‖L²(B) ≤ ρ almost everywhere in time, for a sufficiently small fixed positive cap ρ.

The cost retains the terminal-position tracking square, the fourth power of the L⁴(0,1;L¹²(B)) state norm and the L¹(0,1;L²(B)) control penalty. The quadratic control penalty is zero. An additional terminal-velocity penalty ν‖yₜ(1)‖²H⁻¹(B)/2 is allowed for every fixed finite ν ≥ 0.

For target d = πe, where e is the normalized first radial Dirichlet eigenfunction, zero is the unique global optimizer and its ordinary critical cone is {0}. Nevertheless, the feasible pulses uₕ = he·1{|t−1/2|<h} converge to zero in L∞(0,1;L²(B)), have squared L² norm 2h³, and have objective gap (π²/3 + 2/π²)h⁴ + O(h⁶). Thus strong control-L² quadratic growth fails in both L² and L∞ neighborhoods.

Global optimizers exist for every terminal target d in L²(B) in this capped setting. Along dε = (π+ε)e, every global optimizer satisfies ‖uε‖L²/ε → ∞. Local growth in the L¹(0,1;L²(B)) norm survives. Relative to the fixed zero optimizer, nearby targets give ‖u‖L¹ = O(ε) and ‖u‖L² = O(√ε); on the radial ray, ‖uε‖L¹ = Θ(ε) and cε³ᐟ⁴ ≤ ‖uε‖L² ≤ C√ε.
why_it_works: Classical energy and Strichartz estimates make the nonlinear state close to the linear wave for small control mass: the state is O(‖u‖L¹), and the nonlinear remainder is O(‖u‖⁵L¹). This estimate is in a compatible energy-and-Strichartz state space; it does not assume that the nonlinear solution stays in one eigenmode.

The first eigenmode gives an explicit sine kernel for the terminal linear response. At the midpoint in time, the tracking gain exactly meets the sparse-control threshold. A cap-constrained moment estimate proves global optimality of zero, while pulses concentrating at that midpoint make the quadratic-growth quotient vanish.

The terminal tracking square also provides a weaker L¹ quadratic lower bound. A separate pulse comparison for perturbed targets yields the lower response bounds for every optimizer. These arguments use analytic estimates; the accompanying finite algebra checks are not a numerical solution of the nonlinear PDE.
limitations: This is a counterexample to retaining the ordinary critical-cone implication unchanged when the quadratic control penalty is removed. It does not rule out adapted sufficient conditions, enlarged cones, nondegeneracy assumptions or growth in weaker norms.
The ordinary critical cone is zero, so strict positivity there is vacuous. The result should not be described as a counterexample with a uniformly positive Hessian on every control direction.

The control cap is pointwise in time on the spatial L² norm. It is not a pointwise bound on |u(t,x)|. Here L¹ and L∞ mean time norms with values in L²(B), while control L² is the time-space L² norm. The state penalty remains present; “unregularized” refers to removing the quadratic control term.

The construction uses the three-dimensional unit ball, the defocusing quintic, zero initial data, a small positive cap and a particular target. It does not assert the same failure for every domain, every target, arbitrary large caps, Neumann conditions or boundary control.

The cap and base-target lower bounds can be chosen independently of ν. Upper target-response estimates and their neighborhood are uniform in finite ν; the radial lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. No assertion concerns ν = ∞.

The response estimates compare optimizers with the fixed zero optimizer. They do not prove perturbed-optimizer uniqueness, a pairwise Lipschitz selection, L∞ convergence of perturbed optimizers, or a sharp exponent for the L² response.

The paper gives no certified numerical PDE constant or numerical value of the small-cap threshold. Its finite checks do not replace the analytic proof. The historical question and earlier mechanisms are attributed without a worldwide-firstness or present-day-openness claim.

background.title: Kunisch and Meinlschmidt, Optimal control of an energy-critical semilinear wave equation in 3D with spatially integrated control constraints
background.note: The source model, energy/Strichartz estimate, ordinary critical cone and positive-quadratic-control sufficient condition; see Lemma2.9 and Theorem4.17. Published in J. Math. Pures Appl.138 (2020),46–87.

background.title: Meinlschmidt and Kunisch, Optimal Control of a Semilinear Critical Wave Equation (Oberwolfach2021)
background.note: Printed pp.438–440 state the historical question about zero quadratic control regularization, and include the optional terminal-velocity term. This paper addresses the unchanged implication, not every possible unregularized theory.

background.title: Blair, Smith and Sogge, Strichartz estimates for the wave equation on manifolds with boundary
background.note: The classical bounded-domain wave estimates underlying the source model; the L⁴-time/L¹²-space estimate applies in three dimensions.

background.title: Herzog, Stadler and Wachsmuth, Directional Sparsity in Optimal Control of Partial Differential Equations
background.note: Prior group-sparsity and subgradient calculus. The present construction does not claim that threshold mechanism as new.

background.title: Casas and Tröltzsch, Second Order Optimality Conditions and Their Role in PDE Control
background.note: Example4.16 reproduces Dunn’s earlier counterexample to exact-cone sufficiency; broader noncoercivity phenomena predate this wave realization.

background.title: Christof and Wachsmuth, No-Gap Second-Order Conditions via a Directional Curvature Functional
background.note: Prior nondegeneracy conditions account for normalized directions that converge weakly to zero.

background.title: Borchard and Wachsmuth, Second-order conditions for spatio-temporally sparse optimal control via second subderivatives
background.note: A second-subderivative framework distinguishing positivity from the additional nondegeneracy condition; original preprint arXiv2311.14538v1.

background.title: Wachsmuth and Wachsmuth, Second-order conditions for non-uniformly convex integrands: quadratic growth in L¹
background.note: Prior weaker-norm quadratic-growth theory. The paper’s fixed-basepoint estimate is an explicit estimate within its chosen wave example.

collaboration: I welcome independent scrutiny from researchers in PDE-constrained optimization, critical wave equations and nonsmooth analysis, especially of the state-space estimates, the critical-cone interpretation and the quantifiers in the target-response bounds. Substantive verification, improvements to the exposition or a meaningful extension could support a joint journal submission. Authorship would reflect actual contributions.
followup_rationale: No follow-up is proposed. The exponent bracket is not claimed sharp, and this scope pass establishes neither a compelling new mechanism nor novelty for a sharpened result. Generic boundary-condition or parameter variations do not meet the requested bar.
author: Alec Kriebel
